In patients with impaired renal function or low lean body mass, the maintenance dose of digoxin should be adjusted by estimating creatinine clearance (CrCl) and measuring serum digoxin levels. 2. In heart failure, higher dosages of digoxin do not provide additional benefits and may increase toxicity due to reduced renal clearance. 3. In geriatric patients, lean body weight should be used to calculate the digoxin dose, and lower doses within the therapeutic spectrum are recommended for heart failure treatment. 4. When switching from oral or intramuscular (IM) formulations to intravenous (IV) therapy, reduce the digoxin dose by 20-25%. 5. Squill and digoxin exhibit pharmacodynamic synergism, increasing each other's toxicity. This combination is contraindicated. 6. Adagrasib increases digoxin levels or effects by inhibiting the P-glycoprotein (P-gp) efflux transporter. Avoid coadministration or use an alternative drug. 7. Aluminum hydroxide increases digoxin levels or effects by raising gastric pH. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. Avoid coadministration or use an alternative drug. 8. Amiodarone increases digoxin levels by approximately 70% for oral digoxin and 17% for IV digoxin by inhibiting P-gp and competing for renal tubular clearance. Measure digoxin levels before initiating amiodarone and reduce oral digoxin doses by 30-50% and IV doses by 15-30%. 9. Amphotericin B deoxycholate increases digoxin effects through pharmacodynamic synergism, particularly in the presence of hypokalemia. Avoid coadministration or use an alternative drug. 10. Atenolol and digoxin may reduce each other's toxicity through an unspecified interaction mechanism but can increase the risk of bradycardia. Avoid coadministration or use an alternative drug. 11. Avoid use with oral drugs dependent on threshold concentrations for efficacy. 15. Bretylium increases digoxin toxicity through adrenergic effects, including elevated blood pressure and heart rate.
